title: Building synthetic cell-cell synapses using engineered scaffold protein condensates.
authors: Shin, Nick Y; Mitra, Gaurav; Grodsky, Ania M; Ruff, Kiersten M; Chauhan, Gaurav; Pappu, Rohit V; Lim, Wendell A
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Synaptic assemblies that form at cell-cell junctions are often organized by multivalent scaffold proteins with condensate forming properties. An emerging hypothesis is that these scaffolds provide a thresholding mechanism whereby small increases in the density of cell-cell recognition receptors can trigger all-or-none assembly selectively at the correct partner cell interface. We test this hypothesis by engineering synthetic scaffolded synapses. Coarse-grained simulations suggest that properly-tuned scaffold interactions can yield a sharp condensation threshold. Guided by these simulations, we designed modular scaffold proteins consisting of PDZ domains and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of different molecular grammars. Within a specific region of parameter space, controlled by valency, receptor binding affinity and IDR-driven condensation, the synthetic scaffold proteins exhibit switch-like condensation behaviors, where co-condensates of receptor and scaffold selectively form only at interfaces with the proper partner cell. Notably, orthogonal receptor-scaffold pairs enable a single receiver cell to form multiple distinct interfaces, each associated with a different partner cell. We demonstrate that these synthetic synapse assemblies can recruit different client proteins to enhance intercellular signaling, orient cell division, or sculpt complex synaptic morphologies. Our results illustrate how the ultrasensitive condensation properties of modular scaffold proteins can be harnessed to create novel and highly specific cell-cell interfaces.

title: Generative design of functional disordered regions in a developmental transcription factor.
authors: Denes, Lance; Emenecker, Ryan J; Wang, Nongyun; Chirumamilla, Devi; Mohotti, Rashmi; Holehouse, Alex S; Holt, Liam; Lionnet, Timothee
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Rapid advances in protein structure design have not translated to intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). This is largely due to our incomplete understanding of how IDR sequence encodes function. Here, we use stem cell differentiation as a model to map functional sequence features in the C-terminal IDR of the transcription factor RUNX2, which is required to bind chromatin and regulate gene expression during osteogenesis. Surprisingly, linear IDR motifs are dispensable; instead, the conformational dynamics of the IDR predict function. We develop an algorithm for rational IDR design based on biophysical principles, and use it to generate functional IDRs de novo . These findings extend generative protein design beyond the folded proteome.

title: TSL-phosphorylated SGS3 shifts RDR6 from terminal nucleotidyltransferase to polymerase activity to promote RNAi and immunity.
authors: Li, Niankui; Athukorala, Kisalka; Oh, Tae Rin; Li, Changhao; Zhong, Songxiao; Yang, Yizhou; Choi, Suk Won; Peng, Xu; Zhang, Xiuren
abstract: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase 6 (RDR6) and suppressor of gene silencing 3 (SGS3) form small interfering RNA (siRNA) bodies to synthesize double-stranded RNA, triggering RNA interference. Like viral RDRs, RDR6 not only has polymerase action but also has terminal nucleotidyltransferase activity that tails single-stranded RNA templates, causing their degradation. How the dual activities are controlled is unknown. Here we discovered that Arabidopsis Tousled (TSL) predominantly phosphorylates Ser65 and Ser68, located in the intrinsically disordered region of SGS3, to promote RNA interference. SGS3 phosphomimics trigger the formation of liquid-like siRNA bodies but have lower RNA-binding affinity, thereby enhancing RDR6 polymerase activity to synthesize double-stranded RNA for downstream processing by Dicer-like 2/4. Conversely, hypo-phosphorylated SGS3 forms larger and solid-like aggregates that hold RNA templates with stronger affinity, thereby prompting RDR6 terminal nucleotidyltransferase activity. Moreover, viral infection drives SGS3 hypo-phosphorylation and aggregation, suppressing viral siRNA production and host defence. Collectively, stoichiometric phosphorylation of SGS3 switches two distinct activities of RDR6 to tune RNA silencing and host anti-viral immunity.

title: Computational Structural Dynamics and Preliminary Heterologous Expression Suggest a "Rigid-Anchor, Flexible-Melting" RNA Chaperone Mechanism for Rice OsCSP1.
authors: Liang, Yue; Zhang, Jinyi; An, Xinyi; Kong, Ying; Xu, Liangyuan; Liu, Jian; Zhao, Fei; Wu, Jiang
abstract: Cold and drought are major abiotic stresses that severely constrain rice (Oryza sativa) growth and productivity. Cold shock proteins (CSPs) act as RNA chaperones that facilitate post-transcriptional adaptation under environmental stress. In this study, we combined phylogenetic analysis, prokaryotic heterologous expression, and all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to elucidate the evolutionary features, stress-protective capacity, and working mechanism of rice OsCSP1. Promoter analysis revealed enrichment of low-temperature responsive (LTR) and MYB-binding drought-responsive (MBS) cis-elements upstream of OsCSP1. Heterologous overexpression of OsCSP1 in Escherichia coli showed no cytotoxicity at 37 degrees C. Under 17 degrees C cold stress, recombinant strains overcame initial metabolic burden and exhibited superior biomass accumulation (OD600) compared with empty vector controls during late log phase. Spot dilution assays indicated enhanced colony-forming ability at 10(-3) dilution. Sector-plate assays further demonstrated strong induction-dependent cytoprotection against both prolonged cold (17 degrees C) and 15% (w/v) PEG6000-induced osmotic stress in E. coli, highlighting its potential protective efficacy in heterologous systems. AlphaFold 3 modeling of the OsCSP1-U6 RNA complex yielded a moderate interface confidence (ipTM = 0.66), which is expected for proteins containing intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Subsequent 100-ns all-atom MD simulations revealed rapid contraction in radius of gyration (Rg) and solvent-accessible surface area (SASA), forming a compact, solvent-resistant conformation. RMSF analysis showed a rigid N-terminal CSD anchor coupled with a highly dynamic C-terminal IDR. MM/PBSA binding free energy decomposition indicated that the interaction is primarily driven by van der Waals and electrostatic forces. We propose a "rigid-anchor, flexible-melting" model in which the CSD is predicted to provide stable RNA binding while the flexible IDR is hypothesized to facilitate the destabilization of misfolded RNA secondary structures. These findings provide a foundational biophysical framework that facilitates future in planta functional validation of OsCSP1 as a potential target for engineering climate-resilient rice.

title: FE65 Recognition Rewires the Dynamic Contact Network of the Amyloid Precursor Protein Intracellular Domain.
journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
abstract: The amyloid precursor protein intracellular domain (AICD) is a short, intrinsically disordered signaling fragment that mediates interactions with adaptor proteins involved in APP trafficking and transcription-associated regulation. Among these partners, FE65 recognizes the conserved YENPTY-containing region of AICD, yet the ensemble-level mechanism underlying this interaction remains unclear. Here, we use molecular dynamics simulations to compare unbound and bound AICD together with YENPTY-motif mutant variants. In the unbound state, AICD samples a heterogeneous conformational ensemble dominated by disordered states while retaining transient local structure and recurrent intramolecular contacts. Upon FE65 binding, AICD does not collapse into a single rigid conformation; instead, its conformational ensemble is redistributed toward interaction-compatible substates. Residue-resolved contact analyses identify localized interaction hotspots within and adjacent to the YENPTY region, including aromatic and polar residues that dominate the bound-state contact network. Mutations within the YENPTY motif alter the balance between compact and extended conformations while preserving the intrinsically disordered character of the peptide. Together, these results support a recognition mechanism in which FE65 binds a partially organized AICD ensemble via localized interaction hotspots and ensemble reweighting, rather than through complete disorder-to-order folding. This work provides a molecular framework for understanding APP intracellular-tail recognition and its regulation by sequence-localized perturbations. More broadly, these findings illustrate how intrinsically disordered motifs can achieve specific molecular recognition through redistribution of dynamic contact networks without undergoing complete disorder-to-order transitions.

title: Spatial control of karyopherin binding avidity within NPC mimics revealed by designer FG-nucleoporins.
authors: de Vries, Hendrik W; Barth, Anders; Fragasso, Alessio; Otto, Tegan A; van den Berg, Ashmiani; van der Sluis, Eli O; van der Giessen, Erik; Veenhoff, Liesbeth M; Dekker, Cees; Onck, Patrick R
abstract: Nucleocytoplasmic transport occurs via nuclear pore complexes (NPCs), ~40-60 nm wide pores lined with intrinsically disordered proteins that are rich in Phe-Gly motifs (FG-Nups) that form a selective barrier. Molecules larger than ~50 kDa are increasingly blocked for transport unless they are bound to a nuclear transport receptor such as the karyopherin (Kap) family of proteins. How the amino acid sequence of FG-Nups contributes to this selectivity is not fully understood. Here, we present de novo designed artificial FG-Nups with a systematically varied FG-repeat spacing and charge-to-hydrophobicity ratio (C/H). Starting from a reference sequence termed NupY (with the average properties of yeast GLFG-Nups), we design, synthesize, and experimentally test a library of NupY variants using quartz crystal microbalance with dissipation monitoring and phase separation assays. We find that the spacing between FG-motifs governs Kap95 absorption into the FG-Nup phase, while increasing C/H results in higher avidity for Kap95 due to an increased accessibility of FG-motifs. Molecular dynamics simulations of transport through NupY-coated pores show a reduced barrier function for noncohesive variants and the highest transport selectivity for designs close to native GLFG-Nups. We postulate that a balance between steric hindrance and enthalpic gain from multivalent Kap-FG-Nup interactions drives the spatial and temporal partitioning of Kaps in the NPC.

title: Targeting P23 by PM534 suppresses glioblastoma via disruption of SFPQ-mediated phase separation.
authors: Lu, Xuxiu; Wang, Hui; Zhang, Aotong; Zhang, Qun; Cao, Qun; Hou, Chuanke; Li, Zhuo; Guo, Chenghui; Li, Ping; Fu, Yitong; Chen, Anjing
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is one of the most lethal human malignancies, with a five-year survival rate of approximately 5% and limited effective therapeutic options beyond standard-of-care regimens, underscoring an urgent need for novel therapeutic agents and druggable targets. Here, we report that PM534, a marine sponge-derived synthetic compound, potently suppresses GBM malignancy in orthotopic patient-derived xenograft (PDX) models and in vitro, with IC(50) value of 1.86 nM in patient-derived GBM#P3 cells. Target identification via activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) revealed P23, a co-chaperone of HSP90, as the direct molecular target of PM534. Subsequent LC-MS/MS analysis, molecular dynamics simulation, and site-directed mutagenesis collectively demonstrated that PM534 covalently bond P23 at Cys58 and Cys75. P23 demonstrated significant upregulation in human GBM tissues and orthotopic PDX models, correlating with tumor progression. Mechanistic studies exhibited that P23 interacted with splicing factor proline- and glutamine-rich protein (SFPQ) to regulate liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS). Covalent engagement of P23 by PM534 disrupted the interaction of SFPQ with the HSP90/P23 complex, thereby triggering proteasomal degradation of SFPQ and consequently abrogating SFPQ-driven LLPS and oncogenic condensate formation. These findings establish PM534 as a promising drug candidate for clinical GBM therapy and highlight P23 as a therapeutic target in GBM.

title: Cancer-associated histone tail mutations reshape conformational ensembles and DNA-contact states in nucleosomes.
authors: Wang, Liujin; Zhang, Houfang; Yuan, Xupeng; Mai, Meiru; Zhao, Yunjie; Peng, Yunhui
abstract: Cancer-associated histone mutations can perturb chromatin regulation, yet how many noncanonical mutations in intrinsically disordered histone tails alter nucleosome dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we combine pan-cancer histone mutation profiling with 31.5 mus of all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of complete nucleosomes to investigate recurrent mutations in the H2A, H2B, H3, and H4 tails. We identify recurrent and understudied mutation sites beyond canonical H3 oncohistones and characterize how selected substitutions perturb histone-tail conformational ensembles and DNA contacts in their nucleosomal context. The simulations reveal mutation-specific redistribution of tail-DNA contacts across the nucleosomal DNA surface, accompanied by changes in MM/GBSA-derived relative interaction-energy estimates. For selected systems, Markov state modeling further resolves metastable tail-DNA contact states and shows that mutations alter their structural characteristics and population distributions. These perturbations are not confined to the substituted residues but extend to neighboring interaction networks. Together, our results provide a molecular-level physical picture of how cancer-associated histone-tail mutations reshape conformational and interaction-state landscapes in nucleosomes.

title: Molecular Grammar of Microtubule-Wetting Condensates.
authors: Muthachikavil, Aswin Vinod; Allolio, Christoph; Seal, Ayush; Kuhne, Thomas D
abstract: Microtubule-condensate interactions regulate cytoskeletal dynamics involved in cell division, vesicle transport and cellular locomotion. Due to the size of microtubules and the slow timescale of condensate structural relaxation, there has not been a systematic investigation at the molecular level as to what binding patterns (molecular grammar) enable condensate binding to microtubules. We provide a simulation protocol that is able to predict whether any given disordered protein sequence will bind to microtubules. This simulation setup is suitable for compound testing. Our pattern analysis allows us to establish two categories of strongly interacting subsequences that enable binding to microtubules: positively charged hydrophobic clusters and alternating charge sequences. Their overall optimal balance is analyzed and preferential regions of interaction on microtubules are identified and validated with known experimental results.

title: Coacervate droplets as a liquefier for the solid-to-liquid transition of RNA aggregates.
authors: Guo, Wei; Luo, Rong; Shen, Yi; Zeng, Xiangze; Liu, Zhou; Shum, Ho Cheung
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
abstract: Biomolecular condensates are functionally gated by their material properties. While RNA is a primary structural scaffold, its sequence-specific interactions can aberrantly drive condensates into dysfunctional solid aggregates. Yet, actively reversing this solidification to restore function remains a fundamental challenge, impeding progress in synthetic biology and therapeutics interventions. Here, we establish that complex coacervates can be engineered as liquefiers to actively remodel solid RNA-peptide aggregates into functional liquid droplets. Integrating systematic experiments with all-atom simulations, we decode a multiscale mechanism: coacervate infiltration at the micrometer scale mediates molecular buffering at the nanometer scale, which fluidizes the crosslinked network to drive macroscopic liquefaction. This capability is governed by a design rule, where coacervates formed by small-molecular anions exhibit optimal efficacy. We deploy this principle to functionally rescue silenced RNA within a model of pathologically solidified ribonucleoprotein assemblies. Our work provides a general framework for the active, compositional control of biomolecular phase behavior, with direct implications for managing pathological aggregation and engineering functional condensates in synthetic and living systems.

title: A compact generative language model learns the compositional grammar of phase-separating proteins.
authors: Wasim, Abdul; Pramanik, Ushasi; Das, Anirban; Latua, Pikaso; Rudra, Jai S; Mondal, Jagannath
abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of intrinsically disordered proteins drives the formation of biomolecular condensates, yet the sequence-level grammar that promotes condensation remains difficult to specify from first principles. Existing protein language models are typically trained on large, folded-protein-rich sequence corpora and may not optimally capture the compositional biases of LLPS-prone disordered proteins. Here, we show that a compact generative language model, with an architecture and size ( approximately 17 M parameters) selected via systematic hyperparameter optimization and cross-validation, trained from scratch on a small set of phase-separating protein sequences, can learn sequence features associated with condensate formation. The model generates thousands of sequences that reproduce length-dependent trends in disorder, charge decoration, hydropathy patterning, and sequence entropy, with training and generative behavior stable across independent seeds. Homology analysis indicates that generated sequences are not full-length copies of known proteins, but instead combine short segments matching natural proteins with a novel, model-generated sequence. Descriptor-based screening of short generated sequences yielded a pool of disordered candidates, from which five synthetically feasible peptides were selected for experimental testing. Four of them show condensate-like signatures under near-physiological conditions, including droplet-like assemblies and increased turbidity. Coarse-grained phase-coexistence simulations of a subset of generated sequences with longer lengths show a broad range of phase-separation tendencies, with 12 of 89 sequences comparable to the strongly phase-separating hnRNPA1 low-complexity domain. These results suggest that compact, task-specific generative models can learn information-rich sequence grammars from small curated datasets and propose experimentally testable condensate-forming peptides.

title: Switchable hydrophilicity solvents and biosolvents for green microextraction in bioanalysis.
authors: Nisyriou, Styliani; Ntorkou, Marianna; Patakidou, Christina; Zacharis, Constantinos K
abstract: Sample preparation is critical in bioanalysis because of complex biological matrices and low analyte concentrations. Conventional liquid-liquid and solid-phase extraction are effective but often consume substantial organic solvents and resources. Green analytical chemistry has therefore promoted miniaturized microextraction approaches that reduce solvent use and waste while maintaining analytical performance. This review critically examines bioanalytical microextraction through two intersecting solvent-design perspectives: stimulus-responsive switchability and renewable/bio-derived solvent design, focusing on switchable-hydrophilicity solvents (SHSs) and bio-derived deep eutectic solvents (DESs)/natural deep eutectic solvents (NADESs). SHSs enable reversible changes in hydrophilicity or ionic character to facilitate extraction and phase separation, whereas bio-derived DES/NADES systems provide tunable alternatives to conventional petroleum-based solvents. Their analytical performance, matrix-related challenges, reproducibility, and greenness are critically assessed. Future developments are expected to emphasize automated and miniaturized platforms, life-cycle assessment, and computationally assisted solvent design. Although molecular simulations are increasingly used to support solvent selection, predictive COSMO-RS and artificial-intelligence approaches remain emerging directions in bioanalysis.
